item.title: You Can't Think Your Way Out of Anxiety
item.description:
Anxiety

You Can't Think Your Way Out of Anxiety

Regulation must come before reasoning.

Posted September 22, 2026

Key points
  • Anxiety is more than excessive worry.
  • A person cannot effectively think their way out of a nervous system that feels unsafe.
  • Effective treatment for anxiety requires a holistic approach.
Source: Adobe free stock image by Lightfield Studios

It is time to move beyond telling people with anxiety to simply stop worrying about the future.

A recent Psychology Today blog post by Neel Burton offered a Stoic perspective on anxiety. As a fan of Marcus Aurelius, I appreciate the value of Stoic wisdom. However, relying on it as the primary response to anxiety can misrepresent the condition’s underlying causes. It may also leave people feeling worse when they cannot simply “let go” of their worries.

As a psychotherapist who has worked with many clients experiencing anxiety, and as someone personally familiar with this unwelcome and worrisome guest, I find this oversimplification disappointing and frustrating. Ancient wisdom can be helpful, but it may not be sufficient on its own. Anxiety is not merely “worrying too much.” It involves central nervous system hyperarousal and complex interactions among the amygdala, prefrontal cortex, hippocampus, autonomic nervous system, and stress hormones.

This understanding of anxiety requires us to broaden our treatment options. Stoic philosophy, yogic practices, and modern teachings about the “power of now” can all have a place in the toolbox. Yet, in my personal and professional experience, simply recognizing that anxious thoughts arise from within rarely provides enough control over the intense symptoms generated by a dysregulated nervous system. Even a simple breathing exercise can feel out of reach when someone no longer feels able to press the pause button in either mind or body.

An estimated 6.8 million Americans experience generalized anxiety disorder in a given year. Approximately 2.9 million may use some form of complementary health approach, including:

  • Mindfulness meditation
  • Yoga
  • Breathing exercises
  • Massage therapy
  • Biofeedback
  • Acupuncture
  • Guided imagery and relaxation training
  • Spiritual or faith-based practices

These estimates highlight what many people with anxiety already know: No single approach works for everyone. Many are willing to try almost anything to escape the persistent dread and fear that can occur when the nervous system becomes stuck in fight, flight, or freeze mode. If philosophical reflection alone were sufficient, we would expect greater calm in our increasingly anxious world. Instead, rising distress suggests the need for a more complete, holistic approach.

article continues after advertisement

A Biopsychosocial Approach

Current best practice for central nervous system dysregulation uses a biopsychosocial approach. It combines physiological regulation, such as sleep, exercise, and breathing; psychological interventions, such as cognitive behavioral therapy and mindfulness; social connection; and medication when appropriate.

The goal is not to eliminate anxiety entirely, but to restore nervous system flexibility and resilience. In practical terms, this means helping the mind and body respond to genuine threats and return to calm when the threat has passed.

Regulate Before You Reason

Treating anxiety requires understanding how the central nervous system functions and how to help it regain balance. A multimodal approach begins not with trying to control worried thoughts, but with calming an overactive autonomic nervous system. This is the principle of “regulate before you reason.” Foundational practices include:

  • Improving sleep hygiene
  • Engaging in regular aerobic exercise
  • Limiting excessive caffeine and alcohol
  • Stabilizing blood sugar through regular, balanced nutrition
  • Maintaining adequate hydration

These practices help stabilize the body when the brain’s reasoning centers are less accessible because the amygdala, the brain’s threat detector, and the hypothalamus, a key stress activator, are highly engaged.

article continues after advertisement

Breathwork and Body-Based Regulation

Breathwork can be an important part of regulating the central nervous system and reducing anxiety. Common evidence-informed practices include:

  • Slow diaphragmatic breathing
  • Extended-exhalation breathing, such as inhaling for four seconds and exhaling for six to eight seconds
  • Coherent breathing at approximately five to six breaths per minute

These techniques can help shift the body from a reactive stress state toward greater calm. Yoga, qigong, massage, biofeedback, and somatic therapies may further strengthen a person’s ability to feel safe and grounded in the body.

When Reasoning Becomes More Accessible

As physiological arousal decreases, the prefrontal cortex, which supports reasoning and self-regulation, can become more accessible. Cognitive behavioral therapy can then help with:

  • Reducing catastrophic thinking
  • Challenging the overestimation of threat
  • Building tolerance for uncertainty
  • Decreasing avoidance behaviors

Medication as One Option

When anxiety is so intense that even a list of coping strategies feels overwhelming, medication may be worth considering. Consultation with a qualified medical professional can help determine whether medication is appropriate and how it might support the healing process.

A More Compassionate Understanding

As we learn more about the neurophysiology of anxiety, it becomes increasingly clear that anxiety cannot be reduced to a failure of willpower or perspective. Helpful wisdom still has a place, but the most compassionate and effective response begins with understanding the nervous system, reducing physiological arousal, and then helping the person think, connect, and act with greater flexibility.

item.title: What Is Love?
item.description:
Philosophy

What Is Love?

How to distinguish true love from mere dependency.

Posted September 22, 2026

Key points
  • Romantic love inherited many of the expectations once placed upon religion.
  • Asking one person to provide everything makes disappointment inevitable.
  • Love enlarges one's world; dependency asks another person to fill it.
To grow, the lobster must first shed its shell.
Source: Wikimedia Commons/Jan de Heem/Public domain

When worldly ambition fails to validate us, we often turn to romantic love. We rely on another person to lend our life weight and meaning. First, we ask the crowd; then, we ask one person.

The Greeks had several words for love: eros, philia, storge, and agape. Eros is passionate love, philia is friendship, storge is familial love, and agape is universal love. But we reduce all these types of love into just one word, which we associate with romantic love.

The Rise of Romantic Love

What we don’t realise is that romantic love, unlike passionate love, is a fairly modern concept. If you think about it, romantic love barely features in the 73 books of the Bible. The Bible’s greatest love stories are David and Jonathan, Ruth and Naomi, and, above all, the love of man for God. In the ancient world, passionate love was not seen as ennobling but as a dangerous affliction: think only of Helen and Paris, Dido and Aeneas, Antony and Cleopatra.

How, then, did this dangerous affliction become our highest ideal? As religion retreated, our need for religion remained. We still longed for meaning and transcendence. Gradually, the sacred seeped out of God and into romantic love. We stopped loving God and began loving love.

That’s why love speaks the language of religion: adoration, devotion, eternal union. We expect one person to provide us with everything: intimacy, friendship, intellectual stimulation—until death do us part.

What Love Really Is

But once a person is given the role of God, disappointment becomes inevitable. When things go wrong, we conclude that we chose the wrong person, or that love has died—not that we are asking far too much.

This brings us back to the original question: What is love? Beneath all its forms—philia, eros, storge, agape—love is a reaching out beyond ourselves towards someone or something that lends weight and meaning to our life. It is the force that enables us to cross the boundary between ourselves and the world—to shed our shell, like a lobster, and grow beyond it. That’s why people of little love are so small.

This definition of love is useful, in that it gives us a litmus test by which to distinguish love from mere dependency. We can ask: Is this person enlarging my world, or am I merely asking them to save me from myself? Are we growing together, or merely leaning against one another?

item.title: Two Brains in One: Rethinking Split-Brain Models
item.description:
Neuroscience

Two Brains in One: Rethinking Split-Brain Models

A new study upends long-held beliefs about the brain's origin and development.

Posted September 22, 2026

Key points
  • New research suggests the developing brain arises from two distinct neural progenitor lineages.
  • Mouse and human stem-cell studies reveal parallel tracks for the forebrain/midbrain and hindbrain.
  • The findings challenge the traditional single-origin model of brain development and its evolution.
Source: Lightspring / Shutterstock

For centuries, neuroscientists have operated under a foundational assumption: The human brain is a single, contiguous organ. Anatomists have long believed that as an embryo develops, a single progenitor cell line branches out, smoothly differentiating into the forebrain, midbrain, and hindbrain.

A new study from Stanford Medicine upends this prevailing model. Published September 18, 2026, in Nature Neuroscience, this groundbreaking research suggests that what we call the human brain is actually two ancient, distinct nervous systems.

According to the recent findings, these separate but parallel organs each evolved independently over hundreds of millions of years, eventually melding into a split-brain entity that functions as a single, whole brain.

The researchers call them anterior neural ectoderm and posterior neural ectoderm. The anterior population gives rise to the forebrain and midbrain; the posterior population gives rise to the hindbrain. The two lineages also have distinct chromatin landscapes, suggesting that their developmental fates become established remarkably early.

As someone who's spent decades exploring the interplay between different brain regions, I contend that this cutting-edge discovery has paradigm-shifting potential. It also provides a fascinating new biological context for the vertical "split-brain" framework I first proposed in The Athlete's Way back in 2007.

Split-Brain Frameworks: Moving from Left/Right to Up/Down

Pop psychology in the 1970s and 1980s was dominated by another split-brain model: the left brain/right brain dichotomy. Rooted in Roger Sperry's Nobel Prize-winning split-brain research, the cultural interpretation quickly morphed into an overly simplified personality test.

Under this framework, people were classified as either "left-brained" (logical, analytical, mathematical) or "right-brained" (creative, intuitive, artistic). Bestselling books like Betty Edwards' Drawing on the Right Side of the Brain (Tarcher) cemented the interhemispheric divide of left brain/right brain in the public imagination.

This rudimentary illustration shows how split-brain models divide the human brain from east to west and north to south within the whole brain.
Source: Photo and illustration by Christopher Bergland (Circa 2009)

While the two hemispheres of the cerebrum do have functional asymmetries, the pop-culture binary was always a bit of a stretch. When I was conceptualizing the neurobiology of sports and human performance for The Athlete's Way in the early 21st century, the left-right model didn't fit my lived experience. My father, a neuroscientist who taught me to play tennis in the 1970s, constantly emphasized the role of the cerebellum (Latin for "little brain") in motor learning, muscle memory, and superfluid coordination.

article continues after advertisement

To counteract the left-right craze, I shifted the axis 90 degrees from an east-west orientation and proposed a vertical, north-south split-brain model: the cerebrum represented the "up-brain" (conscious thought, cognitive control) and the cerebellum represented the "down-brain" (automatic movements, intuitive flow), with the midbrain acting as the equator connecting the two hemispheres.

A Different Kind of Split Brain

Notably, the Stanford researchers didn't unearth a cerebrum-versus-cerebellum split; that wasn't the focus of their research. Instead, they found two developmental lineages that arise in parallel rather than one common neural ectoderm lineage branching into all major brain regions.

Using lineage tracing in mouse embryos, the researchers found that the anterior neural ectoderm population, marked by Otx2, was committed to forebrain and midbrain fates. A second population, associated with Gbx2, was committed to forming the hindbrain. Experiments with human pluripotent stem cells showed the same basic commitment: Cells placed on one developmental track could not simply be redirected into the other.

That helps explain why scientists had struggled to generate certain hindbrain neurons in the laboratory. Using this developmental roadmap, the team generated functional human hindbrain motor neurons corresponding to rhombomeres 5 and 6, cell types that had previously been difficult to produce in vitro.

The researchers also found evidence that this two-lineage organization may be extraordinarily ancient. Comparable anterior-posterior patterns appeared in chickens, zebrafish, and acorn worms, leading the authors to propose that the dual-progenitor architecture may have been conserved for roughly 550 million years.

article continues after advertisement

Interestingly, these two developmental tracks are mutually exclusive from the earliest stages of development. Their DNA chromatin configurations are fundamentally different, locking them into separate fates "like travelers on parallel tracks that never cross," according to a Stanford Medicine news release by Krista Conger. The findings suggest that evolution may have brought two ancient neural systems together into the integrated brain we have today.

While the up-brain/down-brain shorthand may be medically imprecise in light of these discoveries, the new developmental evidence offers an intriguing biological parallel to the north-south divide I was trying to capture. Rather than a single developmental system, the brain appears to emerge from two distinct neural lineages that ultimately function as one integrated organ.

Two Ancient Lineages, One Integrated Brain

In conventional developmental neuroanatomy, the cerebellum is classified as a hindbrain structure. It develops from the metencephalon, a subdivision of the embryonic hindbrain.

To the best of my knowledge, the Stanford researchers didn't specifically trace the cerebellum in this study. Their developmental divide is defined more broadly: anterior neural ectoderm gives rise to the forebrain and midbrain, while posterior neural ectoderm gives rise to the hindbrain.

Even if the Stanford researchers aren't explicitly seeking to rewrite historical split-brain frameworks, the implications for how we view whole-brain functions are likely to keep evolving. Whether we're looking at higher-level cognition or the superfluidity of athletic mastery, our capacities rely on the integration of brain regions shaped by two ancient developmental tracks that ultimately function as one.

The brain isn't a monolith; it's a multifaceted partnership. The more we learn about how these two ancient systems cooperate, the better we can understand how our cranial globe bridges hemispheric divides. The brain may look like one organ, but its evolutionary history tells a more complicated story.

item.title: How to Build Your Self-Discipline
item.description:
Self-Control

How to Build Your Self-Discipline

Neuroscience shows that the life you seek is hidden in the discipline you avoid.

Posted September 22, 2026

Key points
  • Difficulty builds discipline only when there is a real impulse or preference to overcome.
  • Society's modern conveniences give fewer chances to practice delaying reward and tolerating discomfort.
  • Deliberate practice builds self-discipline; choose harder paths to handle internal resistance.

Imagine two people who take a cold shower—James and Jimmy:

  • James loves cold showers; he takes them all the time, especially when recovering from exercise.
  • Jimmy hates the feeling of cold water, but he’s heard of the benefits to mental and physical health.

Who is practising more self-discipline by taking the cold shower?

Jimmy, because he doesn’t want to have a cold shower. In fact, James doesn’t require any self-discipline to take a cold shower; he may be doing something physically difficult, but there isn’t any internal conflict to overcome.

The interesting thing here is that if you don’t find it difficult, it doesn’t require self-discipline. So perhaps we need to distinguish between two kinds of difficulty:

  1. Objective difficulty: How demanding is the behaviour itself?
  2. Psychological difficulty: How much internal resistance must you overcome to do it?

What does this do to your brain?

Researchers have found that the anterior midcingulate cortex plays an important role in tenacity—our ability to persist towards a goal despite the effort or discomfort involved. [1]

Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) studies have associated greater anterior midcingulate cortex activity with greater persistence and willingness to exert effort. [1-3]

Neuroscientist Andrew Huberman’s interpretation is that the anterior midcingulate cortex is strengthened when you repeatedly do things you don’t want to do. [4]

And that’s the key: To build the muscle of self-discipline, you have to consistently do things you genuinely don’t want to do. In other words, doing something difficult because you already enjoy doing it is psychologically different from doing something difficult while part of you is telling you to stop.

In a world where comfort and convenience are at our fingertips, how often do we win that battle?

We can now choose from more films or meals than ever before and have them arrive in front of us on demand. When we feel bored, we can satisfy our urge to be entertained in an instant by opening any of a hundred apps on our phone.

article continues after advertisement

The instant access we have to immediate rewards goes directly against the nature of self-discipline:[5]

Doing the things you don’t like to do for an extended period of time without getting a reward.

When immediate gratification was less readily available, everyday life contained more unavoidable periods of waiting, effort, and frustration. Those experiences challenged us to practise self-discipline.

With the comforts of modern living, we may be giving this system fewer opportunities to be challenged—and I think we can sense it. Perhaps that helps explain the appeal of books like Do Hard Things by Steve Magness and Yes Theory’s slogan: Seek discomfort.

Before we rebuild our self-discipline, we need to be clear on our why

Without a clear reason to be self-disciplined, there’s no counterweight against the force of temptation when it arises.

For example, if you require self-discipline to resist eating unhealthy food, you need to be clear on your purpose for doing so. It could be to improve your physique, lower your risk of a health condition, or simply feel better. However, without knowing what to be disciplined for, you’ll be far more likely to give in to the temptation because its benefits will be unopposed by any greater benefit.

In Discipline is Destiny, Ryan Holiday describes this as having a purpose so you can avoid temptations that distract you from that purpose.[6]

This sense of purpose might be easy to imagine when choosing between something as consequential as keeping your job and having a lie-in every day. But even for smaller habits like the urge to check your phone while someone is speaking to you, perhaps you’ve decided that being present in your relationships is a stronger why than satisfying every flicker of curiosity.

This also explains why discipline without direction can become pointless. The goal isn’t to make your life unnecessarily unpleasant or deny yourself everything enjoyable.

The goal is to become capable of tolerating discomfort when doing so protects something you value more.

Now that we know why we should choose self-discipline, how can we build it?

article continues after advertisement

It’s funny how we deliberately practise skills like speaking a language, playing a musical instrument, or mastering a technical skill for work, yet most of us haven't thought to deliberately practise a skill as far-reaching as self-discipline.

Maybe that’s because it’s hard to imagine. What would deliberate practice for self-discipline even look like?

Simply put, we need to create safe situations where self-discipline is required by doing something worthwhile despite not feeling like doing it. Ryan Holiday encourages us to look for opportunities to make life less pleasant, such as by taking the stairs instead of the lift or exercising without listening to any music to hype us.[6]

Choosing the harder path for yourself when it's safe and controlled gives you practice tolerating the same internal resistance that appears when the stakes are higher.

In the example of taking a cold shower, as Wim Hof argues in The Wim Hof Method, by training yourself to handle the cold through repeated exposure, you train yourself to handle other kinds of stress, too.[7]

This is particularly important when overcoming stressors that you already know are hard for you. For example, if you feel uncomfortable being on stage, the next time you get the chance to do something similar, like karaoke, volunteer yourself. This will be difficult, but that’s the point. By familiarising yourself with a feeling that would normally make you retreat, you will build the resilience to overcome that feeling when you cannot avoid it in the future.

Even Seneca, despite possessing great wealth, would deliberately practise living in poverty by sleeping on a hard surface and eating basic food to make sure he could still live freely without his riches.[8]

What healthy action will you take today that you'd rather not do, purely to practise self-discipline?

item.title: Understanding Proposal Anxiety
item.description:
Marriage

Understanding Proposal Anxiety

Are you ready to propose? How do you know?

Posted September 22, 2026

Key points
  • Anxiety does not tell you whether a decision is right or wrong.
  • Understanding anxiety is the best way to regulate it.

According to the Knot’s 2026 Real Weddings Survey, about 40% of the proposals that are made in a year occur between Thanksgiving and Valentine’s Day, with the most popular month being December. This means early fall is a time of really important consideration. For many, it might also mean a lot of doubt and anxiety. Maybe you already have the ring and a proposal plan, but are hesitating. To move forward with confidence, you are going to have to address your anxiety. Ignore it and it will only intensify.

It is easiest to engage with an emotion if you understand what it is trying to do. All emotions are here to help us, even if they are uncomfortable. To work through proposal anxiety, there is one main question you need to ask yourself: What is the anxiety trying to tell me?

This question is easier to answer if you understand the function of anxiety. Anxiety, like all emotions, communicates and motivates. Having anxiety is usually an indication that something is new or important, or that something is uncertain. Which of these three categories is true for you? Is it more than one?

If proposing is a new experience, maybe you need to review your plan. Set some details for yourself and see if that helps. Check in with friends or family members who have proposed and ask for some tips, or even just their story if you are trying to keep your own plans more private. There are more unknowns in things that are new. Invite in some more certainty and reassess your anxiety.

If proposing feels overwhelmingly important, I would say that's an accurate assessment. Your anxiety may reflect you wanting to get it right. Connect with the value, and validate the emotion yourself: It's doing its job. Acknowledgement of how you feel is likely the best option. Let the anxiety motivate you to put some more effort into your proposal.

If you are uncertain about whether or not this is the right decision, review the facts and your motivations. Anxiety can be an imprecise communicator, which is why it is important to understand its function. Anxiety craves certainty. It will set off alarm bells if it senses there is something unknown about the future. Managing uncertainty is part of life, which is why you also need to regulate anxiety when making decisions. Decision limbo is often more painful than any decision you end up making. To work with anxiety about uncertainty, you will have to accept that no human is all knowing.

Now that you have listened and hopefully determined what anxiety is latching on to, you are ready to regulate more actively.

Regulating anxiety requires you to first slow down. Anxiety about important decisions motivates us to withdraw, procrastinate, seek reassurance, or avoid. This slowdown in behavior can be helpful as long as you use that extra energy to actually make a decision. Beware the behavior loop. Have you read 1 or 2 articles on proposal anxiety, or more than 10? If it's the latter, you are probably stuck in a loop. Anxiety will motivate you to continue reviewing and seeking information until you achieve 100% certainty—but that does not exist.

After you have slowed down, made your list of pros and cons, and talked to others, stop gathering more information. Make the decision and commit to it. If you want a more involved proposal plan, pay any necessary deposits and hire the photographer to capture the moment. If you are going to be a bit more spontaneous, tell someone you trust to carry around the ring so you are ready. There will be less room for anxiety to creep in and cause more doubt if action quickly follows the decision.

How can I be sure proposing is the right decision?

Still seeking reassurance? The answer is you cannot be sure it is the right decision. There is a leap of faith that comes with proposing. Sometimes you just have to decide. If you are unwilling to accept some uncertainty, maybe you are not ready. A life committed to another person will be full of unknown adventures. This is just the first one.

article continues after advertisement

Anxiety does not tell you whether decisions are wrong or right. Being anxious about major decisions matches the situation. Hopefully understanding a little bit more about anxiety itself helps you interpret its message a little more effectively.

item.title: Is Skinny 'Kinda Chic?'
item.description:
Body Image

Is Skinny 'Kinda Chic?'

Though body ideals have shifted over time, thinness is making a comeback.

Posted September 22, 2026

Key points
  • Cultural standards of beauty and body types are cyclical and shift over time.
  • Social media content strongly influences people's self-concept and feelings about their bodies.
  • Weight stigma remains constant in society and can lead to unhealthy attitudes and behaviors.
Source: Monika Kozub/Unsplash

The current “kinda chic” craze has gone viral on social media. The good part is how it pokes fun at the mundane while acknowledging the importance of setting healthy boundaries and developing self-acceptance. Shifting the focus away from overly pretentious content is also a welcome change in the age of AI and enhanced images. It demonstrates that we can appreciate everyday reality instead of performing with fake personas.

Yet, this trend is also connected to the ways we internalize an appearance-focused mindset and the relationship we have to our bodies.

Ideals of Beauty in the 1960s

If you grew up in the 1960s, you probably remember supermodels like Jean Shrimpton, Verushka, and Twiggy. These famous faces and figures revolutionized the fashion industry and influenced cultural standards of beauty.

The curvier, more voluptuous shapes of women in the 1950s were replaced with less feminine, reed-thin bodies. Women strove to emulate this look, which was an unrealistic goal for the vast majority. This carried over into the dance community, as the Balanchine aesthetic of a long, lean, slender body type became the ideal standard for female ballet dancers. It also set the stage for unhealthy eating behaviors, the development of clinical eating disorders, and an intense striving for the elusive notion of perfection.

The Influence of “Heroin Chic”

This “skinny worship” trend eased up somewhat in the 1970s and 1980s, with feminists rejecting the notion of an ideal body type. Many fashion models in the 1980s, including Cindy Crawford and Christie Brinkley, had curvier, more athletic builds.

The 1990s, however, glamorized the “heroin chic” look. An extremely thin physique, pale skin, dark under-eye circles, and disheveled hair and clothes (Smith et al., 2023) were considered to be cool. Do you recall the sickly appearance of model Kate Moss in the ubiquitous Calvin Klein ad? It was disturbing to see a drug-addicted, anorexic image being encouraged and normalized. In a 2009 interview, Moss remarked, “Nothing tastes as good as skinny feels,” but since regrets making that comment (BBC, 2018).

What’s Old Is New Again

Appearance-focused outlooks have shifted over the past decade. The Kardashians rebelled against the lean body type by demonstrating hourglass body proportions reminiscent of the 1950s. Ballet dancers, such as Misty Copeland and Sylvie Guillem, also personified a more muscular build than what was typical.

article continues after advertisement

However, the idea of “thin is in” seems to be making a comeback in the 2020s, which is a significant cause for concern. The media is saturated with photos of underweight celebrities out and about on the Red Carpet, such as Ariana Grande, Demi Moore, and Cynthia Erivo. We can take these role models seriously and try to replicate their look, or we can view it as an opportunity to examine and resist these exaggerated stereotypes.

On a positive note, more celebrities are speaking out about their mental health struggles and battles with eating disorders. Nonetheless, we often detect mixed messages when they claim to be recovered and healthy, while we can clearly see their emaciated bodies.

The Weight Loss Obsession

When do the scales tip from thinness as a form of beauty to manifesting as an unhealthy obsession?

The revival of “heroin chic” as a mainstream concept today has the potential to increase substance abuse disorders, eating disorders, and body dysmorphic disorders (Smith et al., 2023). The recent surge in popularity of GLP-1 weight-loss medications is a prime example of the endless pursuit of thinness.

In one study, despite the potential risk factors and side effects, individuals who reported body shame, body surveillance, disordered eating, higher BMIs, weight concerns, and fat-shaming were most likely to try GLP-1 medications (Markey et al., 2025). Many celebrities have shared their satisfaction with the number of pounds they have lost on GLP-1 treatments. While these products are highly effective for weight loss, they can lead to the onset or return of restrictive eating patterns (Richards & Khalsa, 2024). Additionally, their widespread use perpetuates the stigma that fat is unattractive, and we should strive to be thin.

Finding Your Own Self-Concept

So, if you think being skinny should be portrayed as chic or “kinda chic,” weigh in and take a closer look at the ways these concepts have evolved. Decide for yourself if this resonates with your self-concept, authenticity, relationship to your appearance, and how you want to present yourself to the world.

article continues after advertisement

Cultural norms will continue to go in and out of fashion. With millions of influencers on social media trying to shape our bodies, opinions, and behaviors, it’s hard to know who to follow. We don’t have to keep up with the latest flavor-of-the-month, but we should keep an open mind, be discerning, and keep cultivating a strong sense of self. Consider the wise words of Dolly Parton: “Find out who you are and do it on purpose.” Now, that’s “kinda chic!"

item.title: How Frayed Edges in Strong Relationships Are Self-Repaired
item.description:
Relationships

How Frayed Edges in Strong Relationships Are Self-Repaired

In a strong relationship, the person who was let down might do the repairing.

Posted September 22, 2026

Key points
  • Strong relationships are not just smooth and salubrious. Small failures keep getting repaired.
  • The aggrieved party minimizes the effect of the lapse through biased cognitive processing.
  • The more salubrious form of this process works only for minor failures, and with trust already in place.
Relational repair
Source: Elio Santos / Unsplash

Think of a strong relationship, with a person, a company, or an organization at work. Its strength is not that fewer things go wrong. People can be inattentive, colleagues are abrupt, companies make mistakes, and now and then a product we trust disappoints us. What is remarkable in a strong relationship is that some of these lapses get repaired, and even more remarkable is the fact that the person doing the repairing is often the person who was wronged.

Take a colleague you have worked with closely for years. You trust her judgment and expect to keep working together. One day she dismisses something you say too quickly, or is unusually short with you. You notice this, and it bothers you in the moment, but almost right away it starts to get explained away. She has had a hard week. That is not how she normally behaves. I probably caught her at a bad moment.

The same thing happens with companies. I have been loyal to a couple of airlines over the years. When I meet an employee of one of these airlines who is unusually unhelpful, I have the option of treating the encounter as evidence about the airline (a moment of truth, as it might be called), or I might find a way to localize the experience as stemming from one employee, on one day, at an airline I have had a good history with. I still notice the bad experience, but, sometimes implicitly and sometimes quite deliberately, I find a way to minimize it, and even dismiss it from active memory.

Why Aggrieved Parties Initiate Relationship Repair

We typically think of repair as the onus of the offending party, whether in work life, consumer-brand contexts, or even in politics. Recovery takes the route of an apology, an explanation, or a refund. What I am discussing here is something that the aggrieved party does, with or without the offense being recognized or acted upon by the offending party.

One reason this happens is that the relationship itself is valuable. Developing a strong and stable relationship, whether with a colleague or a company, takes time and effort. It often means rejecting other options, so over time the relationship also becomes hard to replace. A strong relationship creates efficiencies, by reducing the time spent in verifying commitments and by not having to spend time and effort repeatedly searching through options when a need arises.

Once a relationship has that value, a small failure creates an imbalance. I believe this is a good colleague, but she has just behaved badly. I believe this is a reliable company, but I have just been treated poorly. Festinger's theory of cognitive dissonance, or Heider's balance theory, describes what happens next. When two beliefs are at odds with each other (great company but poor service attitude today), people are generally motivated to reduce the inconsistency and the lingering negative feeling it creates. One way is to revise the larger belief: Perhaps I was wrong about the person or the company. The other is to revise the meaning of the immediate event: It was unusual, there is another explanation, it should not carry much weight. A long record of reliability probably should affect how we read one bad episode, so this is not irrational.

article continues after advertisement

Ahluwalia, Burnkrant, and Unnava, colleagues when I was at Ohio State, studied how committed consumers responded to negative publicity about a brand. Highly committed consumers counterargued the negative information and held on to their earlier views. Less committed consumers treated it as diagnostic and updated their judgments. Negative publicity is not the same as a service failure one experiences directly, but the mechanism carries over.

Kunda's work on motivated reasoning points the same way. People cannot believe whatever they like, but when more than one interpretation is plausible, their goals influence which one they find persuasive. A trusted person was having a terrible day. The employee was not representative of the company. Other research has found a similar pattern in romantic relationships. Partners hold somewhat idealized views of each other, and those views predict how well the relationship holds up later. In each case the relationship affects how reality gets interpreted.

There is also a plainer reason. In my work, I find that the shadow of the future exerts a strong influence on what happens today. If I expect to keep working with someone, today's irritation gets set aside quickly in service of our collaborative outcomes. If I expect to keep using a company, as in the case of the airline, one bad encounter gets parked so it is not likely to affect my positive expectations for the next flight with the airline.

The Limitations and Potentially Toxic Side of Relational Self-Repair

Volitional self-repair typically works for minor and moderate failures. Repeated failures are much harder to explain away. Serious violations may work differently still. When an event signals dishonesty or betrayal, the closeness of the relationship can make the reaction worse, because more has been invested and more was expected.

The same process, but without the trusted relationship, can also be a concern. A vulnerable customer without access to better alternatives may keep using a company and, rather than live with the resentment, may talk himself into the view that the company is not so bad. In our own research on older patients obtaining medications for chronic disease, consumers with highly restricted choices remained in the exchange relationship despite being bothered by aspects of it. In such cases, what looks like loyalty may partly reflect the absence of alternatives rather than the strength of the relationship.

article continues after advertisement

Within those limits, the case for building trust and strong relationships is usually premised on returns such as loyalty, retention, and recommendation. A strong relationship can also make the customer a participant in maintaining that strength by how they handle one poor encounter, and how they decide to localize its effects. The same is true between people. Sometimes the person noticing a small crack is the one who goes on to mend it. A unique benefit of having earned another person's trust is that the other person may acquire reasons to keep the trust intact.

item.title: Attention, Please: Why Children Need Parents Who Look Up
item.description:
Parenting

Attention, Please: Why Children Need Parents Who Look Up

Digital distraction can interfere with learning and connection.

Posted September 22, 2026

Key points
  • Children notice when screens take priority and may feel ignored or unimportant.
  • Mothers who use less media have richer conversations with their toddlers.
  • Media-free times can protect conversation, responsiveness, and shared family experiences.
Source: Image by StockSnap from Pixabay

This article was coauthored by Daniel Frost and Hailey Holmgren, professors at Brigham Young University, and Esther Eberting, a student at Brigham Young University.

“Mom! Mom! Watch this!”

“Look at what I made!”

“Did you see me, Dad?”

If you’ve been around kids much, you know these kinds of requests occur like clockwork. Kids are constantly asking us to pay attention to them—from proudly showing us a stick-figure crayon drawing to making sure we’re looking before they jump a whole two inches off the ground.

These requests might seem trivial, but child development research shows they may be an instinctual part of children seeking connection. Children want us to see their block towers and somersault attempts because it allows them to learn the social, language, and emotional skills that come from interacting with other humans. Our attention is a powerful developmental tool.

But winning our attention can be a tough battle; today, kids are competing with the endless entertainment and constant interruptions of the digital world. Researchers call it “technoference” when technology interrupts everyday interactions, and parent-child relationships are no exception.

Do these interruptions matter? According to two studies we recently conducted, yes.

Mothers' Media Use and Child Language Development

One study examined how mothers’ digital media use influenced their toddlers’ language environment. We found that mothers who spent the least time on TV, social media, texting, and video games used more descriptive language and engaged in more back-and-forth conversations with their toddlers. In other words, spending less time on devices seemed to create more opportunities for the kind of rich, responsive interactions that help children develop language.

And honestly, it makes sense. Phones so easily divide our attention at just the click of a button or swipe of a screen—even when we’re trying to be responsive. Most of us can probably relate to offering an absent-minded “mm-hmm” before realizing we didn’t quite hear. These distracted moments are normal, but when they become too frequent, young children experience fewer words, fewer conversations, and fewer chances to engage and learn.

article continues after advertisement

Of course, not all media use is equally disruptive. In fact, further results suggested that the type of media used matters, not just how much it’s used. In our study, mothers who used little media, moderate amounts of media, or even high levels of social media and texting spoke more around their children and had more back-and-forth conversations with them than mothers who reported especially high video game use. We can’t say that video games caused these differences, but the pattern suggests that some types of media may pull parents’ attention away from children more than others.

Children's Perspectives on Parental Media Use

A second study also looked at parent media use but instead focused on children’s perspectives. The results showed that not only are children aware of which form of media their parents use and how much, but they’re also opinionated about it. Kids notice when parents’ media use interferes with their relationships, when it becomes overuse, how it impacts their home life, and how it makes them feel.

Kids commented on their parents being on devices “all day long” and told our research team about being ignored or having their requests to play denied, only to see their parent absorbed in a device instead. They described having to ask parents to stop using devices to make breakfast or play with them and getting the dreaded, “Just five more minutes.”

Why Children's Awareness of Screen Time Matters

Why does it matter that kids notice these screen-centered moments? Because from their perspective, screens are prioritized over them. Kids were sad and annoyed at the inescapability of coming up against their parent on a device. They felt replaced by games and videos. They described feeling forgotten or invisible because “Mum is watching her phone” or “Dad was on his tablet” or “They are focused on their games instead of us.”

Whether parents are using devices for video games, Duolingo, family scheduling, or work, these comments point to the reality that children—as oblivious as they may be to their own backward shirt or mismatched shoes—notice their parents’ media use. And they pick up on when their parents choose to spend time on devices instead of with them, often leading to real feelings of sadness and unimportance.

article continues after advertisement
Source: Image by Surprising_Media from Pixabay

Both these findings and those mentioned earlier show that attention may be more important for children’s development than we sometimes realize. Watching your 6-year-old go down the slide or turning away from a new mobile game to talk to your toddler might seem insignificant but can have consequences for their language progression, relationship development, feelings of being valued, and more.

Strategies for Reducing "Technoference"

Families can’t eliminate every instance of technoference, nor do they need to. But they can benefit from clear communication and boundaries around technology use. Parents can be mindful of how and when they use their devices, especially during the moments when children are most likely to seek or need connection. Setting aside media-free times and spaces—perhaps at meals, playtime, or bedtime—can create more opportunities for the conversations, responsiveness, and shared experiences that children crave.

Kids don't need parents who never touch technology. They need parents who watch what they can do, look at what they made, and make them feel seen. They need parents who are fully present when they need them and who have their full attention to offer.

item.title: Goodbye, Gloria, and Thank You
item.description:
Personal Perspectives

Goodbye, Gloria, and Thank You

Personal Perspective: Gloria Steinem sparked my first feminist "click."

Posted September 22, 2026

Key points
  • Gloria Steinem and Ms. magazine emerged as pivotal forces in second-wave feminism.
  • Steinem encouraged women to challenge patriarchal norms and roles.
  • Her efforts led to normalization of women's employment and autonomy.
Source: Photo by Lynn Gilbert via Wikimedia Commons / Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International (CC BY-SA 4.0)

Goodbye, Gloria, and thank you!

We lost one of my heroes this month. If you are a woman in America, or you have ever loved one, you too have lost a great champion—a pioneer who paved the way for women to be treated as fully adult citizens.

In her column in The Chicago Tribune, Heidi Stevens reminds us that Gloria left us a message. She recorded an interview for the Netflix show “Famous Last Words” to air after her death. As always, she teaches us something, leaving us with a task to tell our own stories and listen to others’.

And so, I shall tell my story of how Gloria Steinem and Ms. magazine transformed my life.

I was born in 1956, only a few years before Steinem went undercover as a Playboy Bunny. I grew up as a Baby Boomer, with my first memory of politics being Johnson’s War on Poverty. With two siblings a decade older than me (but still younger than Gloria), I had a bird’s-eye view of the transformation of American colleges from cloistered campuses where young women brought dozens of outfits in hopes of earning "Mrs. degrees" to places of protest against the war in Vietnam, for racial equality and women’s liberation. I watched my strong-willed mother submit to my father’s decisions because that’s just what women had to do.

I watched my male peers prepare for their bar mitzvahs and then be praised at a big party and get lots of presents. Girls got to go to their parties. But women were beginning to demand inclusion in a Judaism that was still unapologetically patriarchal. My parents (surely my mother) must have been a strong advocate because when I insisted girls should have bat mitzvah celebrations as well, and she fought for me, I got a compromise offer: Another girl, Naomi, and I could have a joint event, but not on Saturday morning, and without the signature symbolism of Jewish adulthood, reading from the Torah. We could each chant from the Haftorah (a religious text), but we were not allowed to touch the Torah scrolls; girls were largely still barred from such religious participation in the mid-20th century. We took the offer, but the inequality haunted me. All I could see in the future as a Jewish woman was baking cookies and serving them at the Oneg Shabbat. I wasn’t interested. It was 1968, and this was my feminist “click.”

Discovering Feminism Through Ms. Magazine

Any woman of my generation had a feminist “click”—or one after the other, click, click, click. But what to do about it and how to analyze the underlying misogyny was not nearly as transparent as the sexism itself.

Here is where Gloria and Ms. magazine came in. That same year, Steinem and fellow travelers gave birth to the magazine Ms., and with it, the heyday of the second wave of feminism. I remember that first issue so vividly, with Wonder Woman on the front cover, and the analysis I so desperately needed on the inside. Judaism wasn’t the problem; patriarchy was.

article continues after advertisement

Confronting Patriarchy in Society

And Judaism was hardly the only bastion of male privilege. At that time, there were no women as TV anchors, high-ranking business leaders, politicians, or even principals in schools where the teaching staff was all female. Poor women worked in crappy jobs, and middle-class women with husbands were told their job was to be a helpmate: to raise the children and become an expert at domesticity. Steinem challenged women to be the men their parents wanted them to marry. And that’s what I did.

Women’s employment now is so normalized that it is hard for contemporary young people to understand just how radical it was for women to demand they be treated as fully adult human beings, with the right to education, employment and autonomy.

When I married and kept my own name, I had to carry a marriage certificate with me to rent an apartment, and sometimes even to check into a hotel room. Another fact that 21st-century natives forget: Unmarried couples were considered social deviants and were denied access to everything from nightly to permanent lodging. Gloria Steinem led the charge to end that world.

The Ongoing Fight for Women's Rights

And while we are far from living in a post-feminist world and indeed are in the middle of a terrifying backlash, so much has changed. Judaism now has more female than male rabbis in some denominations. While I was barred from touching the Torah as a child, my own niece is a cantor and leads a large congregation in worship. The majority of rabbinical students are now women, and many are LGBTQ. Women now outnumber men in higher education, although we remain far behind in pay and leadership positions. No one expects women to become Mrs. Him upon marriage anymore, although some may choose to do so. The current administration may want to push women back into their homes, but it is unlikely American women will give up their hard-won autonomy for economic dependence on the man they are currently married to.

article continues after advertisement

We lost Gloria at a ripe old age. She died in a moment of terrifying backlash against women’s freedom. But she has left behind all of us to follow in her footsteps. Her memory will always be a blessing and a call to arms.

item.title: What Do We Do About a Barking Dog?
item.description:
Animal Behavior

What Do We Do About a Barking Dog?

Barking is normal dog behavior. The ethical burden of managing it belongs to us.

Posted September 22, 2026

Key points
  • Barking is normal canine communication, not a malfunction to be silenced.
  • Dogs can't choose their environment, so humans should carry the larger burden of the conflict.
  • Suppressing barking with punishment silences the symptom, not the underlying need.
  • Effective solutions start with the environment and teaching alternatives, not silence.
Source: Robert Gramner/Unsplash

I recently wrote about what's wrong with ultrasonic bark deterrents, particularly when a neighbor aims one at someone else's dog. That piece raised a harder question: if we shouldn't punish a dog for barking, what should we do instead? The practical answer begins with figuring out why the dog is barking. But underneath that practical question is an ethical one, and I think it deserves more attention than it usually gets.

Barking is not a canine malfunction. It's a normal, necessary form of canine communication—dogs bark to alert, warn, greet, protest, express excitement, seek attention, or respond to something that has caught their notice. When barking becomes "a problem," we're really asking a dog to modify a fundamental part of being a dog because of the conditions of human life. And those conditions can be genuinely difficult: enormous numbers of dogs now live in apartments and dense neighborhoods, often just feet from human neighbors, with little room to move, vocalize, or simply be a dog without affecting someone else.

This is a structural problem. And even though nuisance barking often gets framed as a dog-human conflict, more often it's a human-human conflict in which the dog is caught in the middle: The neighbor wants to sleep, the dog wants to bark, and the guardian has responsibilities to both. The ethical question, then, isn't how to quiet the dog. It's how to negotiate competing human interests while minimizing the burden placed on the dog who didn't create any of them.

Not all barking is the same problem

As I noted above, the first practical step is figuring out what kind of barking is actually happening. As trainer Pat Miller has emphasized, identifying the function of the barking should come before choosing a response to it, and Patricia McConnell makes a similar point: a bark might mean anything from put my dinner bowl down to there's a monster in the driveway. That distinction matters ethically, because the same intervention can have very different consequences depending on what's driving it. A dog barking from terror is not having the same experience as one barking because she wants to play, and a device that simply silences barking doesn't distinguish between them; it treats the vocalization itself as the problem, when often the barking is the dog telling us what the problem actually is.

That's the trouble with treating barking like a bad habit to be extinguished: It puts the entire burden on the dog, who has almost no control over the circumstances she lives in. Humans choose the apartment, the schedule, the hours of solitude, the proximity of other people—and then ask the dog to adapt to all of it. Dogs can and should learn to navigate difficult environments, but there's an important difference between helping a dog learn to cope and punishing her for a perfectly normal behavior. A shock, spray, or ultrasonic device may reduce the barking, but silence by itself tells us nothing about whether the dog's underlying needs have been addressed. A frightened dog can become quieter without becoming less frightened. Suppressing something dogs evolved to do, without resolving what's driving it, strikes me as ethically backward.

article continues after advertisement

Taking responsibility without shifting the cost

None of this means neighbors should have to tolerate constant disruption. If your dog is disturbing the people around you, it's your responsibility as her guardian to do something about it—"dogs bark, get over it" isn't a good enough answer, and your neighbors shouldn't have to surrender their sleep or quiet work space because of a choice you made. But taking responsibility doesn't mean making the dog absorb the entire cost. It means looking for solutions that distribute the burden more fairly, starting with the environment rather than the dog herself. If she spends the afternoon barking at passersby, close the blinds or move her away from the window. If fence-line barking is the issue, don't leave her outside for hours rehearsing it. Exercise, enrichment, and rest matter too; management isn't giving in to the dog but changing the circumstances so she isn't spending her day responding to an environment that's asking too much of her.

From there, training can teach a dog what to do after she notices something, rather than teaching her the world is invisible. She's allowed to notice a stranger or hear a noise, and we can help her learn what to do next. McConnell describes an "Enough" cue that means, essentially, move away and come to me, so the sequence becomes: notice, alert, orient toward the guardian, settle. That's a very different message than punishment sends. One teaches the dog how to handle the situation; the other just makes the original behavior costly.

The same logic applies to fear-based barking, which needs distance and gradual counterconditioning rather than suppression, and to barking that functions as a request—for attention, for the door, for a ball—which can often be redirected toward another behavior without eliminating the dog's ability to communicate at all. Teaching a dog to settle, to tolerate stillness without treating every sound as an emergency, helps too. But it's worth holding onto the distinction: Calmness can be learned, while silence can be imposed, and those are not the same achievement.

The conflict belongs to us

Ultimately, this is bigger than dog training. We've built environments in which huge numbers of dogs live in close proximity to people with limited tolerance for canine behavior, and clever training won't make every version of that conflict disappear. What we can do is acknowledge the structural problem and ask who has the power to absorb its costs. The dog has the least. She didn't choose the apartment, the neighborhood, or the three feet separating her yard from someone else's bedroom window. Humans made those arrangements, and so dogs live within social expectations they had no part in setting.

The human guardian should carry the larger share of the work in resolving the conflict—closing blinds, adjusting routines, hiring help, consulting a behavior professional, or simply having an honest conversation with a neighbor about what's being done and when it's hardest for them. That conversation recognizes something worth holding onto: The neighbor isn't the enemy, and neither is the dog. The humans are the ones trying to figure out how to share a world. Once we see it that way, the real question isn't how do I make my dog stop barking, but how do I resolve this without making her pay for a problem humans created.

item.title: Telling People to 'Stop Being Perfectionistic' Doesn't Help
item.description:
Perfectionism

Telling People to 'Stop Being Perfectionistic' Doesn't Help

Asking two simple questions can reshape a perfectionistic mindset.

Posted September 22, 2026

Key points
  • Excellence-seeking perfectionists have high standards; failure-avoiding perfectionists fear making mistakes.
  • Telling people to stop being perfectionist backfires: Some dig in, others polish even more.
  • Treat perfectionism as a mindset, then ask when the setting helps the work and when it hurts it.

Not long ago, perfectionism was a badge of honor. When asked about a weakness, people would say, "I'm a perfectionist." Everyone understood the code: You had high standards.

Now, the same word carries a stigma. Many of my clients complain that their teams are too perfectionistic. People fear showing work in progress, so they keep polishing until they run out of time. By the time leaders see the work, they’re already frustrated—not only because deadlines have slipped, but because it requires more rework.

Perfectionism used to get you promoted. Now it gets you into trouble. But telling people to stop being perfectionists doesn’t help. It rarely works. Sometimes, it can even send the wrong message—as if you want them to rush the work or you don’t care about quality.

Why the Instruction Backfires

Take one of my clients. Decisions were delayed by analysis paralysis. So, the leader pushed back hard: Good enough is better than perfect. Ship it. The more he pushed, the more cautious his people became.

Imagine telling scientists or engineers to stop being perfectionists. How would they react? Probably as if the company thought science wasn’t respected, that data didn’t matter, or the bar was no longer high.

That's because the same instruction reaches two very different people.

One of them sets a high bar because they want to. They catch a defect before it ships, read the contract twice, or notice the number that doesn’t add up. Tell them to stop being a perfectionist, and they hear that the bar just dropped. They hold their ground, and they're right to.

The other one is on their 11th pass at a presentation. They keep polishing because they’re afraid of the review. Tell them to stop being a perfectionist, and they hear that their work is about to be judged. They polish it even more.

Perfectionism has both pros and cons. Excellence-seeking perfectionists are internally driven: They set a high bar and want to constantly improve. Failure-avoiding perfectionists, on the other hand, are driven by others. They fear making mistakes, so they avoid risks at all costs—protecting their self-worth, not necessarily the work.

One instruction, two groups, and neither one gets what the leader meant.

Change the Questions, Change the Conversation

I stopped treating perfectionism as inherently right or wrong. It can work for a team or against it. What matters is how and when you use it.

So I ask teams two questions:

When does perfectionism serve us?

article continues after advertisement

When does it hurt us?

It serves us when it raises the bar. Catching an error before a product ships. Putting a driver's, a patient's, or a passenger's safety over profit. Or being rigorous when the stakes are high enough to warrant it.

It hurts us when we keep polishing because we fear feedback. When we reopen decisions that looked fine a week ago. When we wait for a certainty that isn't coming.

Push for specifics. "Perfectionism slows us down" gives a team nothing. "We spent three weeks on a deck that needed one" gives them something to work with. The more concrete the examples, the more useful the exercise.

If the answers stay abstract, start with a moment instead of the mindset. Name the last piece of work your team failed to launch on time, or the one they shipped too fast and regretted. Ask what people were protecting. Then ask whether it was worth protecting that time.

This exercise moves the conversation from "Stop being a perfectionist" to "Here's where I need to let go, and here's where I'm doing OK." It invites reflection, not finger-pointing. Nobody has to defend their character.

That was my client's real problem. The more he argued against perfectionism, the more his team dug in. Changing the question changed the room.

Change the Conversation, Change the Mindset

Stop treating perfectionism as a personality trait and start treating it as a mindset. "Stop being a perfectionist" sounds like criticism. People need to change their filters, not who they are.

Mindsets are settings of the mind. We can adopt them when they help us and set them aside when they don’t.

In Forward Talk, I argue that the fastest way to change how a team works is to change its conversations—to reframe an obstacle into questions that open up possibilities.

Instead of giving an instruction, ask people two questions: When does perfectionism help us? When does it hurt us? Then, let the conversation begin.

item.title: The Most Dangerous Form of Left-Right Confusion
item.description:
Cognition

The Most Dangerous Form of Left-Right Confusion

A new study focused on the assessment of left-right confusion during surgery.

Posted September 22, 2026

Key points
  • Most people have no problems in distinguishing between left and right, but a minority of people does.
  • Left-right confusion during surgery can lead to patient death or severe injury.
  • The NEST is a new psychological test to assess left-right confusion in a patient-centered model.
  • About 5–10% of people are highly prone to left-right confusion under surgery-like conditions.

Have you ever been confused between left and right in the last month? While most people tend to be able to distinguish left from right, about 10% to 15% of people report that they confuse left and right quite often. This can, for example, happen when driving somewhere and taking a left turn instead of a right turn. While left-right confusion is mostly harmless, there are some situations in which it can be dangerous, or even deadly.

One of these situations is surgery. Imagine somebody has cancer in their left kidney, and this kidney needs to be removed to keep the cancer from spreading. During surgery, however, the surgeon confuses left and right and accidentally removes the healthy kidney on the right side. The patient is left without a functioning kidney. This left-right confusion during surgery is a common form of so-called “Never-Events”, fully preventable medical mistakes that lead to severe injury or death of a patient (Ocklenburg & Petzina, 2026). While psychology has a wide range of research methods and tests (Mundorf and co-workers, 2026), so far, there has not been a specific test for patient-focused left-right confusion in the surgery room. However, since every year, left-right confusion continues to happen in hospitals, it is important to conduct more research on it.

A new test for left-right confusion during surgery

A new study, just published in the scientific journal Frontiers in Cognition, now focused on developing a test to assess left-confusion under similar cognitive dynamics and perspectives as in surgery (Thaler and co-workers, 2026). In the study entitled “Understanding never events: developing an ecologically valid behavioral test for left-right confusion during surgery”, the author team (disclaimer: I have been part of the research team involved in this study) tested 108 volunteers with a new test for left-right confusion, the so-called NEST (Never Events in Surgery Test).

In the NEST, an adult-sized cardiopulmonary resuscitation training doll was placed lying on a medical examination table. Volunteers had to point to specific body parts of the doll under time pressure. Both the posture of the doll (on the stomach, on the back, on the left, or on the right) and the starting position of the volunteers in relation to the doll (from the feet, from the head, from the left, or from the right) were systematically varied. This created different levels of difficulty for the volunteers when distinguishing between the left and right body parts of the doll. For example, when the doll lay on its back, and the volunteers started from a position close to the head of the doll, their left side aligned with the left side of the doll, making the task easy. However, when the doll lay on its back, and the volunteer started at a position close to the feet of the doll, their left side was the right side of the doll. This makes the task much harder.

Additionally, the volunteers were tested with three established psychological tests for left-right confusion: First, the Left-Right Questionnaire, a self-report questionnaire about how commonly the volunteers confused left and right in everyday life. Second, the Bergen Left-Right Discrimination Task, in which volunteers had to look at pictures of stick figures and identify the left and right hands. Third, the Left-Right Commands Task, in which volunteers had to listen to spoken commands and touch their own body parts accordingly (for example: “Touch your left knee with your right elbow!”).

article continues after advertisement

Results of the study: Most people are great at distinguishing left from right, but 5% to 10% are really bad

What did the scientists find out? As was to be expected, most volunteers were great at distinguishing left from right, with more than 50% of the sample not making any left-right confusions in the NEST. However, in each condition, there was a small group of volunteers (around 5% to 10%) that confused between left and right quite often, making four or more left-right confusions. Clearly, these people would not be great surgeons! The volunteers made fewer errors when the doll lay on its stomach than in the other conditions. Importantly, the error rate of the established left-right confusion tests could not be used to predict the number of left-right confusions in the NEST. This suggests that they may not be optimal to assess left-right confusions in situations, especially relevant for treating patients.

Take- Away

Left-right confusion in the surgery room is the most dangerous form of left-right confusion and can potentially result in death or severe injury for the patient. The NEST is an important new psychological test to better investigate and understand why some doctors may confuse their patients' left and right limbs.
